hints: Look closely at the two ends that are joining - what functional groups are on the end of the chain and on the left side of cysteine?
Remember what type of reaction joins two amino acids, and think about which small molecule is always removed when -OH and -H are lost.
Focus on drawing the new link so that the C from the chain joins directly to the N of cysteine, keeping $C=O$ on the left and $N-H$ on the right.
walkthrough:
Spot the Joining Groups**
You have the end of the growing chain with $-C(=O)-OH$ and cysteine with $-NH_2$ shown as $NH$ with two H atoms. Joining amino acids always uses the carboxyl group of one and the amino group of the next.

Remove Water to Make the Link**
Take $-OH$ from the carboxyl group and $-H$ from the amino group to form $H_2O$. This is a condensation reaction. What is left joins together as $C-N$.

Draw the Completed Product**
Extend the chain as ...-box-box-$C(=O)-NH-CH(CH_2SH)-C(=O)-OH$. Show $=O$ still double-bonded to the C, $-H$ still on the N, a single $C-N$ bond between them, and $H_2O$ released.
Final answer: Draw -C(=O)-NH- link between chain and cysteine: chain-C(=O)-NH-CH(cysteine side chain)-C(=O)-OH plus $H_2O$ as product.

hints: Think of the general name for the covalent link that always joins one amino acid to the next in a polypeptide.
walkthrough:
Name the Backbone Link**
Every time two amino acids join by condensation, the $C-N$ link in the $-CO-NH-$ group is called a peptide bond. It forms the backbone of all polypeptides.

hints: Recall where in the cell mRNA is read and tRNA brings new amino acids to the growing chain during translation.
walkthrough:
Locate Translation**
Joining amino acids into a polypeptide is translation. This happens when mRNA and tRNA meet at the ribosome, which catalyses peptide bond formation.

hints: Look at the ribbon shapes in Fig. 1.2 - coils or springs versus flat arrows - what do these two classic symbols represent?
Remember the three possible descriptions of secondary structure, including the thin loop regions that are neither coiled nor flat.
walkthrough:
Read the Ribbon Code**
In ribbon diagrams the coiled spring-like ribbon is an alpha-helix and the flat broad arrows are strands of a beta-pleated sheet. Fig. 1.2 shows both types clearly.

Include the Loops**
The thin string-like parts connecting helices and sheets have no regular hydrogen-bonded shape. They are described as regions of no fixed shape or random coil.
Final answer: Contains alpha-helix / helices and beta-pleated sheet(s) with regions of no fixed shape / random coil.

hints: Start by counting how many separate polypeptide chains make a protein with tertiary structure compared with one with quaternary structure.
Think about where the R-group to R-group bonds are - if there is only one chain, can bonds be between different chains?
walkthrough:
One Chain Means Tertiary**
Tertiary structure is the further 3-D folding of a single polypeptide, held by bonds between R-groups on the same chain. Fig. 1.2 shows one folded chain, so it has tertiary structure.

Why No Quaternary**
Quaternary structure only exists when two or more polypeptides associate, with bonds between R-groups on different polypeptides. Because this protein has only one chain, there are no between-chain interactions, so no quaternary structure.
Final answer: Protein is a single polypeptide / one chain so folded into 3-D tertiary structure; quaternary requires two or more polypeptides with bonds between R-groups on different polypeptides.

hints: Separate the folding into two levels - the initial coiling and pleating, then the overall 3-D folding - what holds the backbone together first?
Now think about what holds the folded shape in place through the side chains, and why cysteine would normally be special here.
List the R-group to R-group interactions that are still possible when no -SH groups are present to form disulfide bridges.
walkthrough:
Secondary Structure - Backbone Hydrogen Bonds**
In an alpha-helix each $N-H$ hydrogen bonds to a $C=O$ three or four amino acids ahead in the same chain. In a beta-pleated sheet each $N-H$ hydrogen bonds to a $C=O$ on an adjacent strand. These are all hydrogen bonds between backbone groups.

Tertiary Structure - R-group Interactions**
The 3-D shape is then held by bonds between R-groups: hydrogen bonds between polar R-groups, ionic bonds between positively charged $NH3+$ and negatively charged $COO-$ R-groups, and hydrophobic interactions between non-polar R-groups tucked inside.

Rule Out Disulfides**
Cysteine has an $-SH$ R-group that can form strong covalent disulfide bridges. Since this protein has no cysteine residues, disulfide bridges cannot contribute, so stability depends on the hydrogen, ionic and hydrophobic interactions above.

Final answer: Secondary held by hydrogen bonds between $C=O$ and $N-H$ of backbone; tertiary held by hydrogen bonds between polar R-groups, ionic bonds between $NH3+$ and $COO-$ R-groups, and hydrophobic interactions between non-polar R-groups; no disulfide bridges as no cysteine.
